title: Immigration and Macroeconomic Outcomes in OECD Countries - Marginal REVOLUTION
gist: A new NBER working paper on OECD immigration 1990-2024 finds the rise in net immigration came predominantly from non-OECD countries and was predominantly high-skilled, that it predicted GDP-per-worker growth mainly through higher investment, and — the sharper result — that native population growth had no or weakly negative effects on GDP per capita and productivity.

themes.theme: Composition of the OECD immigration surge

insights.claim: Across OECD countries over 1990-2024, declining native population growth coincided with rising net immigration, and most of that increase came from non-OECD origin countries and was predominantly high-skilled.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: The marginal OECD migrant is a skilled worker from a non-OECD country, so restrictionist policy bites hardest on the human-capital channel that drives productivity, not on low-wage labour supply.
insights.quote: We compile a new dataset of net immigration rates to OECD countries from all origins and show that most of the increase came from non-OECD countries and was predominantly high-skilled.
insights.locator: OECD countries experienced declining native population growth

insights.claim: Push factors, network effects and policy indices explain little of the large cross-country heterogeneity in immigration dynamics, with unexpected shocks and surges being common.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Migration flows are effectively unforecastable from policy settings — labour-force and housing-demand projections built on immigration policy assumptions carry far more error than they admit.
insights.quote: Push factors, network effects, and policy indices explain little of the large cross-country heterogeneity in immigration dynamics; unexpected shocks and surges were common.
insights.locator: Push factors, network effects, and policy indices

themes.theme: Growth channel runs through investment and TFP

insights.claim: Immigration from non-OECD countries was a significant predictor of GDP per worker growth, operating primarily through higher capital investment rather than through raw labour supply.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Immigration surges should be read as forward indicators of capex, construction and equipment demand in the receiving country, not just as wage-suppression events.
insights.quote: Immigration from non-OECD countries was a significant predictor of GDP per worker growth, primarily through higher investment.
insights.locator: Using local projections and several sources

insights.claim: High-skilled immigration in particular was associated with stronger human capital accumulation, faster total factor productivity growth, and greater capital deepening.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Countries closing skilled-migration channels are trading away TFP growth — a slow-burn negative for their long-run equity risk premium and sovereign growth trajectory.
insights.quote: High-skilled immigration, in particular, was associated with stronger human capital accumulation, faster TFP growth, and greater capital deepening.

insights.claim: Native population growth had no effect or weakly negative effects on GDP per capita and productivity, in sharp contrast to the measured positive effects of immigration.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Undercuts pronatalism-as-growth-policy relative to skilled migration; the productivity payoff is in selection, not in headcount.
insights.quote: Native population growth, by contrast, had no or weakly negative effects on GDP per capita and productivity.
